deck: A tester's pass at every corner of the pdf-tool bridge on this platform: thirteen PDFs — including a fully branded, two-page knowledge-base document with navy/gold color panels, accent bars, and a bordered callout box — ten-plus images, deliberate size-limit violations, bad ids, and every renderer this site has never tried.
description: A live QA pass exercising create_pdf_template, publish_pdf_template, and create_agent_artifact_job across all four renderers and both artifact kinds, with a running log of what broke and what needs finishing.

public.body: This article is the record of a deliberate stress test of this site's own artifact pipeline: how many kinds of PDF and image this platform can actually produce, where the documented limits (like the 150KB image budget) really hold, and what breaks when a tester stops being polite about it.
public.title: Why This Run Exists

public.body: A branded, two-page pdfme document built to match the design bar set by a reference guide: full-bleed navy color panels, a gold accent bar, a bordered callout box, and a manually constructed data grid (the native table plugin never rendered correctly after four attempts — see the findings below for why). This is the ceiling of what this platform's only publishable renderer can do, not the floor.
public.title: Download: Branded Knowledge-Base PDF (2-page, navy/gold, manual grid + callout)

public.body: Across this run, object_create, create_pdf_template, and create_agent_artifact_job each returned a client-facing 60-second timeout or a Cloudflare 502 at least once, yet the underlying write had already landed server-side every time it was checked afterward. That is a dangerous combination for any caller that treats a timeout as ‘nothing happened’ and retries with the same idempotency key or a freshly minted one: a retry against a fixed id correctly hits a conflict, but a retry that mints a new id (the default for object_create) would silently create a duplicate. Reads intermittently returned the same 502s with no side effect, which is the benign version of the same underlying instability.
public.title: Writes That Time Out Anyway Succeed

public.body: pdfme templates work end to end: draft, render, and publish (warn-only gate) all succeeded repeatedly. typst accepted a template body on the first correctly-guessed schema ({source: ‘...’}) but publishing it, and a chromium template, both refuse with a hard gate pointing at validate_pdf_template and get_pdf_template_validation — neither tool is exposed on this connector, Dr_Lurie_Skincare, or Fernwell, so no agent using only these bridges can ever publish a typst or chromium template. react-pdf's template_json schema could not be discovered by informed guessing (a JSX tree, a raw JSX string) in four attempts; the only feedback was the unhelpful ‘Invalid templateJson’, with no field-level detail. Effectively, pdfme is the only renderer an autonomous agent can fully use today.
public.title: Two Renderers Are Reachable, Two Are Not

public.body: object_contract(‘content_item’).media_policy documents over_budget as ‘warn’: an oversize image should be stored and flagged, not rejected. In practice, create_agent_artifact_job hard-fails any image job whose actual output exceeds 153,600 bytes — a 1536x1024 PNG that came in at 156,814 bytes (about 2% over) was rejected outright with no artifact produced at all, and there is no accepted way to raise or bypass that cap from the caller side: passing a top-level requirements.maxBytes override was itself rejected as invalid input. Separately, image size strings are validated against an undocumented allow-list — 1024x1024 and 1536x1024 both work, 256x256 and 512x512 are both rejected as ‘Invalid artifact job input’ with no hint about which sizes are valid. On the positive side, PDF-side requirements.maxBytes is enforced cleanly with a specific, correct error (PDF_REQ_MAX_BYTES, expected vs. actual bytes named explicitly) — that is the error-message quality the image path and the template path should both match.
public.title: The 150KB Image Budget Is Softer in Docs Than in Practice

public.body: list_artifacts_by_kind, search_artifacts, and list_artifacts_by_request — all explicitly documented as admin-only — failed every single call in this session with ‘Authentication token could not be verified,’ including on retries spaced minutes apart. Meanwhile get_artifact_metadata and list_artifacts_for_request, which are not gated as admin-only, worked correctly every time with the exact same credentials. This reads as a scoping or token-audience bug specific to the admin tier, not a general outage.
public.title: Admin Artifact Browsing Is Broken
